content: 1. The study by Onka V et al. focused on reducing pediatric HIV infections by estimating mother-to-child transmission rates in a program setting in Zambia. However, no data were available on mothers who were on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and breastfeeding simultaneously. 2. Van Lettow M et al. examined the uptake and outcomes of a prevention-of-mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) program in Zomba district, Malawi. The study noted that only a very small number of mothers were on ART. 3. Appendix 3 provides descriptive information on studies that included data on breastfeeding and ART. These studies were often embedded within randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and included details such as the place of study, ART initiation, breastfeeding duration, and time of evaluation. 4. The HPTN 046 trial, conducted in South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, evaluated ART and infant nevirapine (NVP) use. Breastfeeding was initiated from the first antenatal visit and continued for six months. The study provided data on HIV transmission rates at six and twelve months. 5. Jamieson et al. conducted a study in antenatal clinics in Malawi, where ART or infant NVP was used alongside nutritional interventions. Most mothers breastfed for 30 weeks or less, and HIV transmission rates were calculated at six and twelve months. 6. The Kisumu Breastfeeding Study in Kenya assessed ART use and breastfeeding for 34 weeks or six months. HIV transmission rates were evaluated at six weeks, six months, and twelve months. 7. Alvarez-Uria et al. studied mothers in India across three hospitals in Antapur. ART was initiated during the first antenatal visit, and breastfeeding or replacement feeding was practiced. HIV transmission rates were assessed at six and twelve months. 8. Peltier et al. conducted research in Rwanda at four government-run health facilities. ART was provided, and breastfeeding or replacement feeding was practiced for 28 weeks or seven months. The study reported overall transmission rates, including peripartum transmission. 9. Marazzi et al. studied mothers in Mozambique, where ART was provided, and breastfeeding continued for 15 weeks or six months. HIV transmission rates were calculated at five months and six weeks. 10. Kilewo et al. conducted a study in Tanzania (Dar es Salaam) where ART was provided, and breastfeeding continued for 34 weeks or six months. HIV transmission rates were evaluated at six weeks, six months, nine months, twelve months, and eighteen months. 11. Sagay et al. studied mothers in Nigeria who were on lifelong ART and breastfeeding. HIV transmission rates were calculated at one year and eighteen months. 12. Ngoma et al. conducted research in Zambia, where ART was provided, and breastfeeding continued for 14 weeks to lifelong. HIV transmission rates were evaluated at six weeks, six months, and twelve months. 13. Appendix 4 outlines the modified Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale. This scale evaluates the quality of studies based on selection, comparability, and outcome categories. It assesses whether exposed and non-exposed individuals are matched and whether confounders are adjusted. 14. The selection criteria assess the representativeness of the exposed cohort, ascertainment of ART exposure, adherence to ART, ascertainment of breastfeeding exposure, and duration of breastfeeding. 15. The outcome criteria evaluate the assessment of HIV transmission, the type of outcome provided (e.g., infection rate with a denominator of children at risk), stratification by feeding type, and adequacy of cohort follow-up. 16. Studies were scored based on whether they provided independent assessments, secure records, or structured interviews for exposure and outcome data. The completeness of follow-up and the adequacy of reporting were also considered.
